p:GMB: The Central Bank of The Gambia issues the dalasi and scores 33 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. The Janneh Commission, a public inquiry into the finances of former president Yahya Jammeh, found that governor Amadou Colley had let Jammeh and General Sulayman Badjie take money out without proper authorisation, including millions of dollars by Badjie. Appearing before that commission on 19 September 2017, Colley said accounts controlled by the Office of the President had been opened at the bank, that an account for sand mining was opened at that office's request, which he called irregular, and that withdrawals followed instructions from an individual in that office without the account signatory's approval. The government's White Paper on the inquiry accepted that between September 2015 and January 2017 Badjie, purportedly acting for Jammeh, instructed the governor or his deputies to release US dollars, and that cash was handed over by the governor to soldiers and loaded into vehicles. It held Badjie accountable for $15,785,601, 300,000 euros and 9,606,000 dalasi and ordered the money recovered by forfeiting and selling his properties, and it also records $28.5 million illegally granted in one bank account in 2000 and 2001 and $268,000 stolen from the bank and used to buy the Observer newspaper. Colley was banned from holding public office for life and held jointly liable for the money taken in breach of the bank's procedures. He had already lost the job by then. On Tuesday 9 May 2017 President Adama Barrow dismissed him along with his deputies Basiru Njai and Oumie Savage-Samba and the bank's director of finance, Ousainou Corr, and no reason was given; Colley said they received their letters that day stating only that their services had been terminated with immediate effect, and that he was surprised at his unceremonious removal after more than three decades of service. The commission was established only in June 2017, a month later, so the dismissal was not a consequence of its findings. Barrow had taken office in January, after Jammeh lost the December 2016 election and left the country under weeks of diplomatic pressure, and had been replacing officials in key positions across a state still largely staffed by Jammeh's allies. The bank's own research economist, Bakary Jammeh, was named governor, and the dismissals came while inflation was high and the dalasi was depreciating. One career move is recorded: Alassan Jabby joined the bank in late 2004 as the accountant in charge of its treasury unit and is now Executive Director and Business Development Manager of FirstBank Gambia Limited, which its own pages describe as a subsidiary of FirstBank of Nigeria Limited, listed on the Nigeria Stock Exchange with over 1.3 million shareholders, so a stock-exchange-listed parent with private shareholders rather than a state bank. De La Rue has printed notes for the bank, and PKF Gambia and PKF Nigeria audited the 2021 accounts.
p:MWI: The Reserve Bank of Malawi issues the kwacha, and presidents have removed its leaders again and again. President Joyce Banda removed governor Perks Ligoya, according to two unnamed sources, with Charles Chuka reportedly chosen to succeed him and no official reason given; the date is not stated. Newly elected president Lazarus Chakwera dismissed governor Dalitso Kabambe and appointed Wilson Banda on 8 July 2020. After a forensic audit of the bank's payments between January 2019 and June 2020, the state charged Kabambe and three others with abuse of office, negligence, money laundering and causing loss of public funds, alleging that 4.3 billion kwacha went to FDH Bank without board approval; pleas were not taken because the charges were subject to change, and nothing is proven. In December 2021 police arrested Kabambe and Joseph Mwanamvekha, saying the two procured and masterminded the falsification of gross liability and net reserve base returns to make the International Monetary Fund believe Malawi was meeting the conditions of its Extended Credit Facility loan; that too stands only as an accusation. Chakwera then dismissed the governor he had himself installed, removing Wilson Banda in early January 2025 and moving up the deputy governor, MacDonald Mafuta Mwale, with immediate effect, subject to confirmation by Parliament's Public Appointments Committee. Mafuta Mwale's own path is the one career move recorded: he had served as Secretary to the Treasury, the senior civil service post in the finance ministry, with no years given for it, and was redeployed back to the Reserve Bank in January of the previous year, two years after that post. The government's statement thanked Banda for his service and gave no reason; Nyasa Times reported that the President had been demanding monetary reforms since June of the previous year and quoted a source close to State House saying the results were painfully slow. Banda had devalued the kwacha by 25 to 27 percent in May 2022, calling it a necessary evil to align the supply of foreign exchange with the fundamentals, and by a further 44 percent in November 2023, and the gap with the parallel market widened after both. A disputed episode runs alongside that removal. Two Malawian civil society organisations, the Black Economic Empowerment Movement and the Forum for National Development, said in January 2026 that the dismissal of the whole board at the time, senior executives included, breached the Reserve Bank of Malawi Act's requirement of continuity in leadership, that they had warned the government the mass dismissal was illegal and left the bank open to manipulation, and that one of those removed, Henry Mathanga, was targeted for perceived political associations rather than misconduct. Nyasa Times reported instead that Mathanga had been removed after a formal disciplinary inquiry under the Act and was facing criminal charges in the Financial Crimes Division of the High Court. The two accounts have not been reconciled. In January 2026 President Peter Mutharika appointed Mathanga deputy governor, and critics say that appointment breaches section 16(2) of the Reserve Bank of Malawi Act. Its 2,000-kwacha note is printed by Giesecke & Devrient, and its accounts for the year ended 31 December 2025, in reports signed on 30 June 2026, were audited by Deloitte in Malawi together with Deloitte & Touche in South Africa. Malawi scores 37 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:URY: Uruguay's money is the peso, issued by the Central Bank of Uruguay and held within a moving band of 2 per cent or less against the US dollar as of December 2025. It scores 19 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it, at 43, although the country scores 73 of 100 on the Corruption Perceptions Index. The constitution has given the executive a hold over the bank's board since 1967. Article 197 provides that where the Poder Ejecutivo, the executive branch, considers the management or acts of the directors of an ente autonomo, a self-governing state body, inconvenient or unlawful, it may make observations and suspend the acts observed, and that if the observations are disregarded it may order the rectifications, correctives or removals it sees fit, reporting them to the Senate. Article 198 adds that it may remove board members with the Senate's consent for ineptitude, omission or crime in office, that if the Senate does not rule within sixty days it may make the removal effective anyway, and that such removals give no right of appeal to the Tribunal de lo Contencioso Administrativo. The Banco Central del Uruguay is an ente autonomo, and article 14 of its charter designates its directors under that same chapter. One case is recorded, from 2017, and it was dismissed: prosecutor Rodrigo Morosoli, investigating the Cambio Nelson fraud at a currency exchange house, sought the formal indictment of Humberto Capote, a former president of the bank, for co-authorship of a continuing crime of misappropriation. Judge Marcelo Souto freed Capote at first instance, finding the evidence insufficient to prosecute him, and the prosecutor appealed in April 2017. No government pressure was reported in the 37 quarters surveyed from 2010 to 2018. Three people have moved between the bank and outside jobs. Guillermo Tolosa confirmed in December 2024 that he would preside over the bank once Yamandu Orsi took office as president of Uruguay; he had worked as an economist at the International Monetary Fund and as a consultant at Oxford Economics, with no years given for either, and was academic director of the research centre Ceres from 2018 to 2020. Washington Ribeiro spent 15 years on the bank's board, as director from June 2010 to March 2020, vice president from March 2020 to July 2024 and president from July 2024 to March 2025, and on 7 April 2026 he started as head of Uruguayan macro and sovereign strategy at the Uruguayan brokerage Latin Securities; no finding or complaint is attached to the move. Diego Labat, president of the bank from 2020 to 2024, was named general manager of the Bolsa Electronica de Valores by its board on 20 August 2025, replacing Eduardo Barbieri after 25 years in the post; the exchange was founded in January 1993 by 26 financial institutions operating in Uruguay, both public and private, so its ownership is mixed rather than plainly private. The accounts are audited by the Tribunal de Cuentas under the 1995 charter law. The bank is also named among the central bank clients of a fixed-income fund built around environmental and social standards, developed jointly by Amundi and the Latin American Reserve Fund; it invests in that fund rather than handing them its reserves to manage. Its notes are printed abroad by Oberthur Fiduciaire, which printed the revised 2,000-peso note dated 2015 that the bank introduced on 27 April 2016, carrying a holographic windowed security thread and a map of Uruguay.
p:MMR: The Central Bank of Myanmar issues the kyat, and the military has taken hold of its leadership. Three days after the coup of 1 February 2021 the military's State Administration Council made Than Than Swe a deputy governor; she later became governor in place of Than Nyein. On 24 August 2022 the junta replaced Than Nyein and a vice chairman with Than Than Swe and Major General Zaw Myint Naing, two months after installing six lieutenant colonels as deputy directors, a shake-up Radio Free Asia reported as a bid to control the country's financial sector. The former deputy governor Bo Bo Nge, arrested on the morning of the coup, was sentenced by a junta court in December 2022 to 20 years in prison after a months-long secret trial, which sources said concerned mismanagement of banks trading foreign currency; the junta-backed Anti-Corruption Commission accused him of not collecting tax on a 5 million US dollar Open Society deposit and of placing a 350 million dollar loan in a lower-interest account, with alleged losses of 102, 360 and 655 million kyats. Those accusations are the commission's own, and the economist Sean Turnell called Bo Bo Nge someone fighting against corruption. Two people have left senior posts at the bank for private banks. Than Lwin was an economist at the bank from 1966, a director in 1997 and deputy governor and controller of foreign exchange from 1997 to 2003, and in 2004 he joined Kanbawza Bank as a consultant, later becoming its deputy chairman; an interview with Kanbawza's senior managing director calls it Myanmar's largest privately owned financial institution and the largest of 19 privately owned banks in the country, which is what establishes the employer's private ownership. Khin Saw Oo, a former deputy governor for whom no central bank dates are given, joined AYA Bank as vice-chairman in 2018 and was re-designated executive chairman in May 2021; AYA's own corporate profile calls it a leading private sector bank in Myanmar and says it was registered as a private company limited by shares on 14 July 2010 and reincorporated as a public company limited on 30 December 2022. No documented case at the bank was found, which is not proof that none happened: Reporters Without Borders rates the situation for journalists here as very serious in its 2026 index, so the court reports and press coverage a case would be found in may not exist or may not be publishable. Government pressure was reported in 18 of 37 quarters between 2010 and 2018, mostly pressing the bank to ease and to print money. Giesecke+Devrient of Munich, which had supplied raw materials, supplies and system components for printing kyat notes, suspended all deliveries to the state-owned Security Print Works after the military crackdown. The bank's own printing works at Wazi printed a 20,000-kyat commemorative note introduced on 31 July 2023, which is not the circulating series, and the Union Auditor General Office audits the accounts under the 2013 central bank law. Myanmar scores 38 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:SSD: South Sudan's money is the South Sudanese pound, issued by the Bank of South Sudan, and its notes are printed by De La Rue, which won a contract for 2.8 billion banknotes in 2011. The country scores 39 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, almost all of it from corruption in the country. A United Nations Human Rights Council commission report said De La Rue transferred about 1.4 million US dollars between 2016 and September 2017 into an Equity Bank account in Nairobi held by a consultant to the bank, against a banknote contract worth about 144 million dollars, and noted suspected corruption. That report stands as an official finding, but the United Kingdom's Serious Fraud Office, which opened its own investigation in July 2019, closed it in June 2020, saying the case did not meet the test for prosecution. On 9 June 2025 President Salva Kiir Mayardit removed Johnny Ohisa Domian as governor by presidential decree, broadcast on state-run media, and no reason was given; the first deputy governor, Addis Ababa Othow, was named to replace him. Othow's own career is the one move recorded here, and it runs in and out of a commercial bank: he joined the Central Bank of Sudan as a banking inspector in 1997, joined Ivory Bank in 1998, came to the Bank of South Sudan in 2010 as head of its non-banking division, headed its planning, regulation and licensing division in 2013, then in 2015 joined Equity Bank's Nairobi headquarters as general manager of operations, becoming managing director of Equity Bank South Sudan in 2018, a step his profile describes as moving back to the private sector; he was first deputy governor from 2022 to October 2023, returned briefly to Equity Bank, was reappointed first deputy governor in February 2025 and appointed governor in June 2025. In February and March 2026 security forces detained former governor Manguak, placed under house arrest, with former finance ministers and other officials, and the information minister said a committee was investigating financial malpractices; no charges had been announced as of March 2026, so nothing is proven, and Manguak denies the allegations. The Auditor General audits the accounts.
p:SLV: El Salvador's central bank is the Central Reserve Bank of El Salvador, and the currency is listed as both the colon and the US dollar. The IMF's 2023 classification puts the country among places with no separate legal tender of their own, using the US dollar as their anchor; legal changes made private acceptance of Bitcoin voluntary and tax payments payable only in US dollars, listed as steps taken before an IMF loan approved on 26 February 2025. One episode with parliament is recorded. In September 2020 Nicolas Martinez, president of the bank, answered a summons from a Legislative Assembly commission investigating the debt the government had taken on during the COVID-19 pandemic and how it was used, and resigned the day after appearing; no reason for the resignation is given. Deputies asked whether the release of banks' liquidity reserve was designed so banks could buy Treasury paper, and he answered that it was an autonomous decision of the banks. Two career moves are recorded. Rafael Barraza Dominguez held the presidency, the vice-presidency and the studies and economic policy management of the bank, with no dates given for any of them, and is now chief executive of Banco Agricola; a rating report filed with the Salvadoran stock exchange states that Banco Agricola's ultimate shareholder is Bancolombia, that the bank belongs to the Banagricola conglomerate owned by Bancolombia Panama, and that the three companies belong to the holding company Inversiones Financieras Banco Agricola, which is what makes this an employer with named corporate shareholders and no state holding. The other move stays within the public sector: Carlos Paredes came to the presidency of the bank from the Autonomous Port Executive Commission, the National Centre for Agricultural and Forestry Technology, the National Council for Science and Technology and the Ministry of Economy, with no dates given and no private financial employer named. No case at the bank is documented, which does not prove none happened; Reporters Without Borders rates the situation for journalists here as very serious in its 2026 index, so the court reports a case would be found in may not exist or may not be publishable. Written independence from government scores 0.789 of 1, and no government pressure was reported in any of the 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. On its reserves, the bank's own document on international reserves management says it joined the World Bank's Reserve Advisory and Management Partnership in 2010, which it describes as advice on reserve management rather than managing a portfolio, and it names no external portfolio manager or custodian, referring only generally to external investment portfolio managers. The Corte de Cuentas de la Republica audits the accounts under a law still in force. El Salvador scores 39 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:BTN: Bhutan's central bank is the Royal Monetary Authority, which issues the ngultrum and keeps it pegged, or fixed, to the Indian rupee; the rupee circulates in the country as well. Its own law lets the government direct it: under the Royal Monetary Authority Act of Bhutan 2010, passed on 2 June 2010 and in force from 22 June 2010, section 149 lets the Royal Government issue such directives to the Authority as it considers necessary in the public interest, after consulting the Governor and reporting them to Parliament. Four of the Board's seven members are appointed by the Government, one of them from the Ministry of Finance, and the Royal Government sets the Governor's salary and the board members' fees. The Governor is appointed by the Druk Gyalpo on the Prime Minister's recommendation and may be removed the same way, but only on a committee finding of permanent incapacity, incapability of carrying out the duties or breach of the code of conduct. The Act repealed the 1982 Royal Monetary Authority Act, and the arrangement is standing, with no end date. An anonymous informer raised a case in October 2014, and the final findings of Bhutan's Anti-Corruption Commission, covering 2014 to 2016, said a former deputy governor had allegedly forged official documents, misused power and concealed earnings from World Bank and Asian Development Bank projects. Those allegations are unproven; the case was forwarded to the Office of the Attorney General, with no later outcome. One career move is recorded, and every post in it is a public one: Dasho Penjore began at the Royal Monetary Authority in 1987, was its Deputy Managing Director from 2003 to 2006, was appointed Chief Chamberlain to the King in 2006, was Chief Executive Officer of the National Pension and Provident Fund of Bhutan, a statutory pension body, and was appointed Governor of the Authority in December 2015. A commemorative 1,000-ngultrum note marking the Fourth King's seventieth birth anniversary was printed by De La Rue, and M/s P.K. Mitra & Company audited the accounts for 2003 and 2004. India opened a swap line, an arrangement to borrow another central bank's currency, of up to 100 million US dollars or its equivalent on 17 March 2016 under the Reserve Bank of India's SAARC framework; its three-year term ran out in March 2019. The bank scores 27 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:SOM: Somalia's money is the Somali shilling, and the Central Bank of Somalia issues it, though the notes are printed abroad: the circulating 2,000-shilling note comes from Sudan's state currency printing works. Two cases are recorded, and both run through one short governorship. Yussur A. F. Abrar came to the bank in 2013 out of private finance, the one career move recorded here: she had worked at a number of international banks, none of them named in that account, held positions at the African Development Bank and was managing director of TLG Financial Services, and reporting on the day she took office calls her a former banker at Citigroup and AIG, which is what establishes the private employers; the ownership of TLG Financial Services is stated nowhere. She replaced Abdusalam Omer and resigned after seven weeks, writing to the president that from the moment of her appointment she had continuously been asked to sanction deals and violate her fiduciary responsibility to the Somali people; she had refused to sanction a contract over frozen government assets with the United States law firm Shulman Rogers, which denied wrongdoing. She resigned about a month before Bashir Ise Ali was reappointed on an interim basis. A July 2013 report by the United Nations Monitoring Group for Somalia and Eritrea, an official finding, said 80 per cent of withdrawals from the bank were made for private purposes, that the governor was key to the irregularities, and that 12 million of 16.9 million US dollars transferred by the accounting firm PricewaterhouseCoopers could not be traced; the bank rejected the allegations. The bank later became a member of the World Bank's Reserves Advisory and Management Program at the IMF-World Bank annual meetings, which its own newsletter describes as technical support, advisory services and a network of global institutions rather than management of its assets, and Deloitte & Touche, Certified Public Accountants in Tanzania, audited the 2024 accounts. Somalia scores 39 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:UZB: The Central Bank of Uzbekistan, created in 1991, issues the country's money, held at a de facto crawling peg to the US dollar as of December 2025, meaning the rate is moved in small steps. It scores 25 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed; outside influence scores 8 and corruption and secrecy around the bank 60. Written independence from government scores 0.862 of 1 on one index and 0.604 on another, and government pressure was reported in 0 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. One case is on record, and the bank found it itself. In its own 2025 anti-corruption report the bank states that disciplinary measures were applied to 10 of its employees over shortcomings found in its 2025 monitoring, that three procurement counterparties were found to be affiliated with each other and their procurement processes were cancelled, and that two existing conflicts of interest among 2,152 declaring managers were resolved. The head of state has also moved against a chairman: on 11 December 2024 presidential press secretary Sherzod Asadov announced that President Shavkat Mirziyoyev had submitted a proposal to the Senate of the Oliy Majlis for Mamarizo Nurmuratov to leave his post as chairman of the bank, which he had held since June 2017, and the announcement gave no reason; under Uzbek law the Senate acts on the president's nomination, so the initiative came from the head of state. The man who took over that day has moved between the bank and the finance ministry: Timur Ishmetov started at the bank as an economist in 2000, worked through its foreign exchange and reserves departments, was First Deputy Chairman of the State Committee for Investments in April 2017, was the bank's First Deputy Chairman from June 2017 to 2019, left to be First Deputy Minister of Finance in May 2019, was Minister of Finance from February 2020 until the end of 2022, was First Deputy Adviser to the President on economic development, investment and foreign trade policy from December 2022, and became chairman of the bank with effect from 11 December 2024. Gold holdings are 431.7 tonnes, 87.5 per cent of reserves. A swap line, an agreement to borrow another central bank's currency, with China was set at 0.7 billion renminbi in April 2011; whether it is in force is not known. The notes are made by Davlat Belgisi, a state production association that the bank lists among its own subordinate organisations, taking in the Tashkent Printing Factory, the Tashkent Paper Factory and the Tashkent Mint.
p:SDN: The Central Bank of Sudan issues the Sudanese pound. It scores 43 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it, at 85. One career move is recorded, and the dated posts either side of it are public ones: Mohamed Khair Ahmed Al-Zubair was Minister of Finance and National Economy from 2000 to 2001, held state minister and planning posts in the finance ministry through the 1980s and 1990s, was Vice President of the Bank of Sahel and Sahara Community, an intergovernmental bank, from 2002 to 2009, and became Governor of the Central Bank of Sudan in March 2011; the bank's own biography of him also lists former board seats, without dates, at the Saudi Sudanese Bank, where he was president of the board, the Financial Investment Bank and the Agricultural Bank of Sudan, and no source states the ownership of any of those three. In October 2025 Sovereignty Council head Abdel Fattah al-Burhan dismissed governor Burai Al-Siddiq Ali Ahmed after a dispute over the rules for buying and exporting gold, and appointed Amna Mirghani Hassan El Toum; deputy governor Mohamed Osman Ahmed Mohamed Khair was dismissed less than two weeks later. Government pressure was reported in 2 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, both times pressing the bank to cut rates or ease and demanding that it print money. Its law scores 0.333 of 1 on one measure of independence, ranking 172 of 191, and it scores 1.5 of 15 on how much it tells the public. Its notes are made in the country: Dabanga reported in February 2019 that Sudan's new 200-pound banknote had gone into production at the Sudanese Company for Currency Printing, a domestic press the prime minister had visited that week, and the report does not state the company's ownership. Who checks its books is the state rather than a firm: the bank's annual report presents its statement of financial position, profit and loss account, statement of changes in owner equity and cash flow statement for the year ended 31 December 2015 as audited by the National Audit Chamber, the body behind the Central Bank of Sudan Act 2002, which requires the accounts to be audited in accordance with the General Audit Chambers Act 1999 without naming an auditor. No documented case at the central bank was found, which is not proof none happened; Reporters Without Borders rates the situation for journalists here as very serious in its 2026 index, so the court reports a case would be found in may not exist or may not be publishable.
p:PSE: The Palestine Monetary Authority is the monetary authority of Palestine, which has no currency listed here; its exchange-rate classification reads no separate legal tender, or currency union. The head of state names its board. On 4 May 2026 President Mahmoud Abbas issued a decree reconstituting the board of directors, acting on a recommendation from the Cabinet and from the Authority's Governor. Three of the eight seats are held by virtue of law: the Governor as chairman, the Deputy Governor, and a representative of the Ministry of Finance, named as Majdi Al-Hassan; the report does not name the law that gives those seats. The Governor himself came to the Authority from finance, and that is the one career move recorded: Yahya Shunnar took over on 4 January 2025, succeeding Feras Milhem at the end of a four-year term, having held public and private sector roles in the Middle East and the United States, among them director at the Palestine Islamic Bank and vice-chairman of Tamkeen Insurance Company; the bank's own 2025 annual report names its shareholders above 5 per cent, the National Islamic Investment Company with 24.85 per cent, the Palestinian Pension Agency with 10.39 per cent, Razan Medical Center with 10.09 per cent, Mr Salah Al-Daghma with 9.59 per cent, Birzeit Pharmaceutical with 8.51 per cent, the Orphans Fund foundation with 7.01 per cent and Aswaq Investment with 5.45 per cent, which makes the shareholding mostly private with a public pension agency among the large holders. One case is recorded, and the Authority is on the receiving end of the money rather than the subject of the finding: in its 2020 annual report Palestine's Financial and Administrative Control Bureau qualified its audit of the Ministry of Finance's consolidated closing account, and one of its findings was that the ministry had not disclosed 2,130,918 dinars that it owed to the Palestine Monetary Authority. The law that created the Authority in 1997, with one reform since 1970, gives it a legal independence score of 0.435 of 1, ranking 155 of 191. Government pressure was reported in none of 37 quarters between 2010 and 2018. The Authority scores 30 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and its weakest side is corruption in the country.
